passage:
January: Tenzin and his wife Gopika sat with their rent receipts in their Pune flat. Relatives kept asking when they'd buy a house. Tenzin felt behind everyone.

March: They met a fee-only financial adviser recommended by a colleague. She showed them how buying and renting each had costs people forget, like maintenance, interest and being tied to one city. Gopika's job might move. They decided to keep renting for now and build savings.

October: They checked their health cover was enough for both of them and started small, regular retirement contributions. At Diwali, an uncle asked again about a house. Tenzin smiled. "Not yet. We have a plan." For the first time, he didn't feel behind.

qa.q: Whom did Tenzin and Gopika meet in March?
qa.a: They met a fee-only financial adviser recommended by a colleague.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel in January, and why?
qa.a: He felt pressured and behind everyone, because relatives kept asking when they would buy a house.

qa.q: What made their decision a thoughtful one?
qa.a: They got professional advice, compared the hidden costs of buying and renting, and considered Gopika's possible job move.

qa.q: How might relatives see the couple's choice to keep renting?
qa.a: Some may think they're falling behind, not knowing the couple has a clear plan for their future.

grounding: Shows a young couple comparing renting and buying, checking insurance and starting retirement saving over a year.

passage: Tushar, beta, listen to your old Siddharth-mama. When I was twenty-five, I thought retirement was for old men. I spent everything: new scooter, trips, dinners. My friend started putting a little aside every month and I laughed at him. Thirty years later, he retired calmly. I had to keep working longer than I planned. It wasn't a tragedy, but I was tired. And when your mami fell ill, we had no health insurance. The hospital bills took years to pay. So when you get your first salary, talk to someone trustworthy about insurance and a small savings plan for later. Not because I'm telling you. Because I wish someone had told me.

qa.q: What did Siddharth-mama spend his money on at twenty-five?
qa.a: He spent it on a new scooter, trips and dinners.

qa.q: How does Siddharth-mama feel looking back on his choices?
qa.a: He feels regretful and tired, wishing someone had warned him to plan earlier.

qa.q: What does he advise Tushar to do with his first salary?
qa.a: Talk to someone trustworthy about insurance and a small savings plan for later.

qa.q: How might Siddharth-mama's friend see his own early choice?
qa.a: He likely feels glad that saving a little each month let him retire calmly.

grounding: Shows an elder urging a young relative to think early about insurance and retirement saving.

passage: Gargi and Ojas had one week to decide on a flat in Kochi before the builder's offer expired. The monsoon had flooded their current rented place twice. The builder's brochure was glossy, and a relative pushed them to sign quickly. Gargi insisted they slow down. They visited the site in the rain and saw water pooling near the basement. They asked a lawyer friend to check the documents and learned the building approvals weren't complete. Ojas was frustrated. "We'll lose the chance!" But Gargi calmly listed what they didn't know. They decided to keep renting another year, and moved to a higher-floor flat. The offer expired. Ojas sulked for a day, then admitted he felt relieved.

qa.q: What did Gargi and Ojas see at the site in the rain?
qa.a: They saw water pooling near the basement.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he said 'We'll lose the chance!'?
qa.a: He was frustrated and anxious that they would miss out on owning a flat.

qa.q: What made Gargi's approach sensible under time pressure?
qa.a: Gargi checked the site in bad weather and had documents reviewed before committing, refusing to be rushed.

qa.q: How might the pushy relative see their decision?
qa.a: They might think the couple missed a good chance, not knowing about the flooding and incomplete approvals.

grounding: Shows a young couple resisting pressure to buy a home and comparing risks before deciding to keep renting.

passage: Minakshi's parents had been hinting for months: 'Rent is money down the drain. Buy a flat.' At twenty-six, with a steady job in Mangaluru, she half believed them. One Saturday she and her elder sister Bhavna sat at the dining table with a notebook and a laptop. They compared: the down payment would empty her savings; the loan instalment would be almost double her rent; and she might move cities for work in two years. Bhavna asked, 'And if you lose your job? Do you have health cover beyond the office one? Have you started any retirement saving?' Minakshi hadn't. She felt a bit foolish. They booked a session with a fee-only financial planner their cousin trusted, rather than the salesman who kept calling. What Minakshi took away was simple: decide after asking the right questions, not because of a family slogan.

qa.q: Whom did Minakshi and Bhavna book a session with?
qa.a: A fee-only financial planner their cousin trusted.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi feel a bit foolish?
qa.a: She realised she had no health cover beyond her office one and no retirement saving, basics she had not considered before a big purchase.

qa.q: What helped Minakshi approach the rent-or-buy question well?
qa.a: Comparing the down payment, instalment and likely moves, checking insurance and retirement saving, and consulting a qualified planner instead of a salesman.

qa.q: How might Minakshi's parents see her not buying right away?
qa.a: They might worry she is wasting money on rent, since they believe buying is always better.

grounding: Shows a young woman comparing renting and buying and discovering gaps in her insurance and retirement planning.

passage:
'Payal, how much of your salary are you putting away?' Indu asked, folding clothes.
'Mumma, I'm twenty-six. Retirement is forty years away.'
'That's exactly why.' Indu sat on the bed. 'Your father and I started at forty-five. We were lucky with his pension. Many people aren't.'
'But I want to travel, and the scooter...'
'Travel. Just decide the saving first, then enjoy the rest without guilt.'
Payal frowned. 'How much, though? Everyone online says something different.'
'I don't know the right number for you. That's why I've made an appointment with Mrs. Kulkarni, the planner at the bank who helped your father. She'll explain the options.'
'And insurance? Office gives me health cover.'
'Ask her whether that's enough if you change jobs. I don't know either. I only know starting early helps.'
Payal laughed. 'Fine. But I'm still going to Meghalaya in March.'
'Go. Bring me oranges.'

qa.q: At what age did Payal's parents start saving for retirement?
qa.a: At forty-five.

qa.q: What does Payal's frown over 'How much, though?' show about how she feels?
qa.a: She is confused and a little overwhelmed by the conflicting advice she sees online.

qa.q: How does Indu handle the question she cannot answer?
qa.a: She admits she does not know the right number and arranges a meeting with a qualified planner, while sharing the general point that starting early helps.

qa.q: How might Indu feel when Payal insists on going to Meghalaya?
qa.a: Amused and accepting; she wants Payal to save first but also enjoy life, as her request for oranges shows.

grounding: A mother and daughter discuss starting retirement saving early and checking insurance with a qualified planner.
